Ben Horowitz on the rap group he started at 18, and why hip-hop became the source material for how he thinks about business:

"I was probably 12 when Rapper's Delight came out... The first one where I was really like, 'Oh, this is gonna be very different,' was when Run-DMC's Hard Times came out. This has a whole other feel to it than anything I've heard."

"The thing that made me locked into hip-hop: I went to school in New York. I have this friend who I grew up with who had gotten shot in the face in some kind of gun accident, and he was blind... I'd call home to my mom: 'Is he gonna be okay?' She's like, 'He hasn't spoken to anybody since he's been shot.'"

"Being a dumb 18-year-old kid, I was like, 'Hip-hop is so great. You can have nothing and you'll rap about your shoes. He needs that feeling.' So I would record the DJ Red Alert and Chuck Chill Out show. Everybody else would be out Saturday night, and I'd be recording. And I would send him the tapes."

"Then I called home to see how he's doing, and they're like, 'Well, he's talking now, but all he'll talk about is hip-hop.'"

"When I went out that summer, we started a hip-hop group called The Blind and Def Crew. Blind and D-E-F. We rapped about being blind. I wrote most of the lyrics: 'The Blind Def Crew, you know we're fly. Three of us, but we got four eyes.'"

"Hip-hop is very business oriented, particularly in the early days. When I started writing on business, so many of the ideas came from those old hip-hop songs. So I started putting the lyrics at the top of the post to give credit where credit was due."

@bhorowitz w/ @MotownIni

US layoff announcements are declining:

US job cut announcements dropped -20% YoY in September, to 43,281, the lowest September total since 2022.

In Q3, planned layoffs fell -36% YoY, to 129,591, the lowest quarterly figure since Q4 2023.

This brings year-to-date announcements down -39% YoY, to 573,195, the lowest since 2022.

This is also the 7th month of 2026 with job cuts below the corresponding month of the prior year.

The tech sector saw the most announcements last month and year-to-date, at 10,799 and 165,925 respectively.

Meanwhile, market and economic conditions accounted for 8,789 announced job cuts in September, or 20% of all layoffs, bringing the year-to-date total to 114,124, the 2nd-highest of any cited reason after AI.

US employers are taking a wait-and-see approach to layoffs.

Ben Horowitz on the midnight phone call from Kanye that turned his CEO barbecue into a studio session:

"I answer and go, 'Ye, what's up?' He goes, 'Hey Ben, I heard you're having a barbecue tomorrow. Can I come?' I was like, 'Sure.' 'Okay, great. And I want to record in your studio.'"

"I'm like, 'Ye, I don't have a studio.' And he goes, 'Okay.'"

"6:30 in the morning I get a call. 'Hey Ben, I'm Kanye's engineer. I'm just calling about the specs on your studio.' I'm like, 'I don't have a studio.' He's like, 'What do you mean you don't have a studio? Kanye is expecting a studio.'"

"I'm like, 'Who do we know who has a studio?' And they're like, 'Howie.' So we call. 'What are you doing, Howie?' 'Watching Netflix.' 'Is that studio you have portable?' 'Yeah.' Long story short, you drove the studio down to my house and we set it up in the room."

"A lot more crazy stuff happened. Ye was playing us the Pablo album... That was a legendary day. No doubt."

Oil flows in the Strait of Hormuz have sharply rebounded:

Persian Gulf crude oil exports surpassed 14 million barrels per day last week for the first time since the Iran War began on February 28th.

This marks an over +210% increase from the ~4.5 million barrels per day low seen in March.

As a result, the 4-week average is up to 14 million barrels per day, the highest level in 6 months.

Persian Gulf crude oil exports have now recovered to ~80% of their pre-war levels.

This comes as the US military has increasingly secured the Strait of Hormuz and established a two-way shipping corridor along the coast of Oman, allowing oil convoys to resume through the waterway.

Meanwhile, refined fuel shipments, including gasoline, diesel and jet fuel, remain at only around 50% of pre-war levels, as these products are more expensive to transport than crude oil and some refineries in the Persian Gulf that were damaged during the early stages of the war have also yet to fully resume operations.

Oil flows are coming back, but the fuel market is still under intense pressure.

AI-related employment is surging:

AI-linked roles have accounted for more than +750,000 new jobs created in the US since 2023, according to LinkedIn estimates.

This surge has been led by data annotators, with +282,000 new positions created, followed by data center jobs at +117,000, and AI engineers at +105,000.

As a result, these 3 categories have accounted for +504,000 new jobs.

AI-related positions also offer significantly higher pay, with a median salary of ~$180,000 on LinkedIn, compared to $80,000 across all jobs.

This comes as the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure, particularly the buildout of data centers, is driving stronger demand for labor.

The AI boom is reshaping the US job market.

BREAKING: US-listed ETFs have attracted +$1.93 trillion in inflows year-to-date, their largest intake in the first 3 quarters of the year on record.

This figure is +$580 billion, or +43%, above the amount recorded over the same period in 2025.

This also puts inflows for these funds at a record +$214 billion per month.

In Q3 2026 alone, they brought in +$771 billion, their largest quarterly intake on record.

At the current pace, US-listed ETFs are on track to exceed +$2.50 trillion in annual inflows for the first time.

By comparison, these funds attracted +$1.50 trillion and +$1.15 trillion in inflows in full-year 2025 and 2024, respectively.

Investor demand for ETFs remains incredibly strong.

Tech and Industrials continue to show positive trends with eye-popping new order readings above 70. Companies with stronger fundamentals are most insulated from macro headwinds. Consumer Stapes has been the weakest by a macro mile.
